text: {"answer": "The passages suggest intermittent fasting can produce weight loss, but mainly through reduced total energy intake rather than meal timing itself. Supporting evidence reports that time restricted eating lowered daily energy intake and produced weight loss over twelve weeks [fasting#0]. An eating window rule was also reported to be easier to adhere to than continuous calorie restriction, and reduced evening snacking accounted for a meaningful share of the deficit [fasting#1][fasting#3]. However, the contradicting evidence is substantial: head-to-head trials matching total calories found no weight loss advantage over continuous restriction across twelve months [fasting#4]. Several studies also report higher dropout in fasting arms, undermining claims of better long-term adherence [fasting#6]. One short-trial account says benefits largely disappear once energy intake is controlled [fasting#7]. A trial also noted greater lean mass loss in the fasting arm [fasting#5]. Overall, fasting appears effective only as a route to a calorie deficit, with its unique advantage unproven.", "confidence": 55, "one_line": "Intermittent fasting may aid weight loss mainly via calorie deficit; calorie-matched trials show no clear advantage over standard restriction."}
